title: Kings and monks
hookLine: rulers have protected the sangha and used it; both are true

cards: A king wants a war. King Ajatasattu of Magadha has decided to attack his neighbors, the Vajjians, and first he sends his chief minister to the Buddha.

Tell him I'm going to attack, the king says, then come back and report exactly what he says. A strange errand: a ruler using a holy man as a source of intelligence. The Buddha doesn't answer the minister directly.
He turns to Ananda, who is fanning him, and asks how the Vajjians live. That's how the discourse on the Buddha's final passing opens: with a king, a war plan, and a teacher who won't simply be used.

teach.h: DO THEY MEET OFTEN, IN HARMONY?
teach.b: The Buddha's questions are about the Vajjians' habits. Do they meet often, and in harmony? Do they honor their elders?
Do they protect their shrines and the holy people living among them? As long as they do, he says, they can be expected to prosper, not decline. The minister draws his own conclusion and leaves.
Then the Buddha gives his monks a matching list for the sangha.

teach.h: STRENGTH IS HOW A COMMUNITY LIVES.
teach.b: The point is quiet but sharp: a community's strength is in how it lives, not in who is fighting on its side.
That's a good lens for the long history of kings and monks, because rulers have done both to the sangha: protected it, and used it. The emperor Ashoka is one well-known case.
His own inscriptions, carved in stone, express remorse over his conquest of Kalinga and speak of a new aim, conquest by dhamma. He supported monks and sent out envoys.

Tradition, especially in Sri Lanka's chronicles, also says royal power was used to expel monks the court judged false. Protection and control arrived in the same hand. Across Asia, the pattern repeats in different forms.

Kings built monasteries and appointed heads of the order. They also leaned on the robe to make their rule look blessed. The Pali texts have a word for the ideal: dhammaraja, a king who rules by dhamma.
History holds rulers who reached for that ideal and rulers who borrowed the title.
Both are true, and the tradition's own texts keep the question open.

how: In some Buddhist countries today, governments still recognize, fund or regulate the sangha, and Buddhists debate how close monks should stand to political power.

a king who rules by the dhamma

games.q: you're the Buddha. a king's minister says the king will attack his neighbors and wants your answer reported back. what do you do?
o: turn to Ananda and ask how those neighbors live.
refuse to speak and send him away.
games.why: he asks Ananda whether the Vajjians meet in harmony, honor elders and protect holy people, and says while they do, they'll prosper.

practice: Think back over the last day or two and find one moment when someone used power: a boss, a parent, a government, a platform, you.
Ask the Buddha's kind of question: did it protect someone, did it use someone, could it have done both? Stay with the picture, breathing, until you can see both sides without rushing to a verdict.

wordCard.voice: Dhammaraja. The ideal king who rules by dhamma. Rulers have protected the sangha and used it, sometimes in the same breath, from Ajatasattu's errand to Ashoka's edicts and beyond.

orig.note: Pali dhammaraja: a king who rules by dhamma; the ideal ruler of the texts.

carryVoice: Your line: protected and used. A community's strength is in how it lives. Back tomorrow, same hill.
